summary:
Allwork.space argues that the labor market has split into "two capitalisms": one where AI substitutes for codifiable, routine white-collar work, and one where AI complements tacit, contextual human judgment. The piece opens with Mark Fisher's "capitalist realism" and contrasts Citrini Research's "ghost GDP" thesis (AI as labor substitute) with Alex Imas' "relational work" thesis (AI as complement that raises the value of hard-to-codify judgment).

Gad Levanon, chief economist at the Burning Glass Institute, ranked each industry's quits rate against its own 25-year history rather than against other industries, producing three tiers that have diverged since 2022. Finance, insurance, information, and professional and business services (FIIPB) sit at the 13th percentile of their own range; the rest of the private economy at the 44th; government, education and health care at the 71st. Levanon attributes "job hugging" specifically to FIIPB, where employment peaked in early 2023 and has fallen since, leaving quitters nowhere to go. He frames the cause as a decline in the labor intensity of white-collar work, beginning as a post-ZIRP correction but still widening in year four.

A Stanford Digital Economy Lab working paper by Erik Brynjolfsson, Bharat Chandar and Ruyu Chen, using ADP payroll data through June, finds no broad economywide displacement but a 19% shortfall in employment for workers aged 22 to 25 in AI-exposed occupations, visible as absent hiring rather than layoffs. A Bank of America Institute report notes Gen Z job switching has overtaken all other generations for the first time since 2021, with the largest pay bumps.

The piece connects this to Tyler Cowen's distinction between automatable intelligence and tacit "Polanyi knowledge," and raises a pipeline problem: if entry-level apprenticeship rungs disappear, where does the next generation's tacit knowledge come from. It references AI bans in high schools and a David Autor randomized trial of 133 patent lawyers.
